skill.name: systematic-debugging
skill.description: Guides a four-phase debugging process for bugs, test failures, performance issues, build failures, and unexpected behavior.
skill.summary: Investigate failures through evidence, root-cause tracing, focused hypotheses, and verified fixes.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: All 38 static findings are false positives caused by template literals, Markdown, ordinary prose, or bounded diagnostic examples. The reviewed files show no malicious command execution, reconnaissance, hidden-file access, or prompt injection. However, root-cause-tracing.md recommends logging environment variables without redaction, which could expose secrets in diagnostic output.

remediation.issue: Debugging guidance can expose secret environment values.
remediation.suggestion: Replace broad environment-variable logging with an allowlist of non-sensitive names and require redaction before diagnostic output is stored or shared.

content.value_statement: Guessing at fixes wastes time and can create regressions. This skill guides evidence gathering, root-cause tracing, focused hypothesis tests, and verified implementation.
actual_capabilities: Guides a four-phase workflow from root-cause investigation through verified implementation.
Structures reproduction steps, recent-change reviews, and evidence gathering across component boundaries.
Traces invalid values backward through callers to identify their original source.
Tests one explicit hypothesis with the smallest practical change.
Provides condition-based waiting patterns and a shell script for identifying test pollution.
limitations: It cannot guarantee a root cause when evidence, access, or reproduction steps are missing.
Its examples require adaptation to the project language, framework, and operating system.
The included shell script assumes an npm test workflow and simple test filenames.
Production containment decisions still require human judgment, monitoring, and rollback planning.

use_cases.title: Resolve a failing test
use_cases.description: Reproduce a failure, separate symptoms from causes, test one hypothesis, and verify the complete test suite.

use_cases.title: Trace an integration defect
use_cases.description: Instrument component boundaries and locate where data or configuration stops matching expectations.

use_cases.title: Review repeated fix attempts
use_cases.description: Assess failed changes, identify hidden coupling, and decide whether the architecture needs discussion.

prompt_templates.title: Investigate a failing test
prompt_templates.prompt: Investigate this failing test systematically: [failure]. Reproduce it, gather evidence, identify the root cause, then propose one minimal fix.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner investigation of a reproducible test failure.

prompt_templates.title: Trace an unexpected value
prompt_templates.prompt: Trace [unexpected value] backward from [failure location]. Identify each caller, the value passed, and the earliest incorrect assignment.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate analysis of a defect deep in a call stack.

prompt_templates.title: Diagnose a component boundary
prompt_templates.prompt: Diagnose [system failure] across [components]. Define safe instrumentation at each boundary, compare expected and observed data, and isolate the failing component.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced investigation of a multi-component system.

prompt_templates.title: Reassess failed fixes
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these failed fixes: [attempts]. Extract new evidence, challenge the current architecture, and define the next single hypothesis with verification criteria.
prompt_templates.scenario: Expert review after three or more unsuccessful fixes.

output_examples.input: A payment test sometimes remains pending after an arbitrary delay.
output: Reproduction: Run the test repeatedly and record completion events and state transitions.
Hypothesis: The assertion races the asynchronous status update.
Minimal test: Wait for the completed state instead of waiting for a fixed duration.
Verification: Repeat the test under load and run the related suite.

output_examples.input: A repository appears in the wrong directory during tests.
output: Immediate cause: Repository initialization received an empty working directory.
Trace: Follow the directory value through each caller to the test setup.
Root cause: Setup state was read before initialization completed.
Fix and verify: Guard early access, validate each boundary, and rerun pollution checks.

best_practices: Share complete errors, stack traces, reproduction steps, and relevant recent changes.
State one falsifiable hypothesis and define evidence that would confirm or reject it.
Create a failing test before implementation and run related tests after the fix.
anti_patterns: Requesting a fix before reproducing the failure or gathering evidence.
Changing several variables at once and losing the ability to isolate causality.
Treating a longer timeout, retry, or symptom patch as proof of root cause.

faq.question: What problems does this skill cover?
faq.answer: It covers bugs, test failures, build failures, performance problems, integration defects, and other unexpected software behavior.

faq.question: Does the skill execute commands automatically?
faq.answer: The guidance may suggest local diagnostics and includes a test-bisection script. Execution depends on agent permissions and user approval.

faq.question: Which languages and frameworks are supported?
faq.answer: The process is language-neutral. Examples use TypeScript, Bash, Git, and npm, so other environments require adaptation.

faq.question: What happens when the failure is not reproducible?
faq.answer: Gather more evidence, add focused instrumentation, record environmental differences, and avoid speculative fixes until a testable hypothesis exists.

faq.question: Can arbitrary timeouts ever be appropriate?
faq.answer: Yes. Use them only for known timing behavior, after waiting for the triggering condition, with a clear explanation.

faq.question: Does this replace testing or code review?
faq.answer: No. It organizes investigation and verification, while tests, review, monitoring, and human judgment remain necessary.
